case_info.scenario: A man in his mid-50s with a medical history significant for pulmonary embolism 10 years prior (previously receiving anticoagulation therapy) presented to the emergency department with 10 days of progressively worsening, sharp, nonradiating chest pain. The pain was present at rest, 7 of 10 in severity, and worse with inspiration. He experienced concomitant exertional shortness of breath, dry cough, and lightheadedness. His cardiac history was otherwise unremarkable. Family history was notable for breast cancer in his mother and his sister, but no known inherited hypercoagulable disorders. In the emergency department, his vital signs were as follows: temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 130/76 mm Hg, heart rate 97/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. Physical examination results were unremarkable, with no cardiac murmurs, rubs, pulmonary crackles, jugular venous distention, or lower extremity edema. Laboratory test results were remarkable for an elevated D-dimer level, an elevated C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a mildly elevated pro-BNP level, but normal levels of troponin and procalcitonin. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with evidence of right heart strain, and a computed tomography angiogram of the chest demonstrated an occlusive pulmonary embolism of the left main pulmonary artery and several peripheral consolidations in the left lower lung field consistent with infarction. The patient started anticoagulation therapy with intravenous heparin. A subsequent echocardiogram revealed bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle and a very large (6.6 × 4.1-cm), mobile, nonhomogeneous, pedunculated mass straddling the tricuspid valve and moving between the right atrium and right ventricle (Figure 1andVideo).

case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

[Clinical case]
A man in his mid-50s with a medical history significant for pulmonary embolism 10 years prior (previously receiving anticoagulation therapy) presented to the emergency department with 10 days of progressively worsening, sharp, nonradiating chest pain. The pain was present at rest, 7 of 10 in severity, and worse with inspiration. He experienced concomitant exertional shortness of breath, dry cough, and lightheadedness. His cardiac history was otherwise unremarkable. Family history was notable for breast cancer in his mother and his sister, but no known inherited hypercoagulable disorders. In the emergency department, his vital signs were as follows: temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 130/76 mm Hg, heart rate 97/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. Physical examination results were unremarkable, with no cardiac murmurs, rubs, pulmonary crackles, jugular venous distention, or lower extremity edema. Laboratory test results were remarkable for an elevated D-dimer level, an elevated C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a mildly elevated pro-BNP level, but normal levels of troponin and procalcitonin. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with evidence of right heart strain, and a computed tomography angiogram of the chest demonstrated an occlusive pulmonary embolism of the left main pulmonary artery and several peripheral consolidations in the left lower lung field consistent with infarction. The patient started anticoagulation therapy with intravenous heparin. A subsequent echocardiogram revealed bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle and a very large (6.6 × 4.1-cm), mobile, nonhomogeneous, pedunculated mass straddling the tricuspid valve and moving between the right atrium and right ventricle (Figure 1andVideo).

Case:
A man in his mid-50s with a medical history significant for pulmonary embolism 10 years prior (previously receiving anticoagulation therapy) presented to the emergency department with 10 days of progressively worsening, sharp, nonradiating chest pain. The pain was present at rest, 7 of 10 in severity, and worse with inspiration. He experienced concomitant exertional shortness of breath, dry cough, and lightheadedness. His cardiac history was otherwise unremarkable. Family history was notable for breast cancer in his mother and his sister, but no known inherited hypercoagulable disorders. In the emergency department, his vital signs were as follows: temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 130/76 mm Hg, heart rate 97/min, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. Physical examination results were unremarkable, with no cardiac murmurs, rubs, pulmonary crackles, jugular venous distention, or lower extremity edema. Laboratory test results were remarkable for an elevated D-dimer level, an elevated C-reactive protein level and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and a mildly elevated pro-BNP level, but normal levels of troponin and procalcitonin. An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with evidence of right heart strain, and a computed tomography angiogram of the chest demonstrated an occlusive pulmonary embolism of the left main pulmonary artery and several peripheral consolidations in the left lower lung field consistent with infarction. The patient started anticoagulation therapy with intravenous heparin. A subsequent echocardiogram revealed bowing of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle and a very large (6.6 × 4.1-cm), mobile, nonhomogeneous, pedunculated mass straddling the tricuspid valve and moving between the right atrium and right ventricle (Figure 1andVideo).

case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.

case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.

case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.

case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.

case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.

case_info.explanation: Right atrial myxoma with partial myxomatous embolism to the pulmonary artery D. Perform a surgical resection of the mass Primary cardiac tumors are rare, occurring in less than 0.1% of patients.1Of these, myxomas are the most common primary tumors. Originating from primitive connective tissues cells, myxomas are benign masses composed of cells within a mucopolysaccharide stroma.1,2They usually occur sporadically but can be inherited and are more frequently found in middle-aged adults, with a greater predilection for women.3The left atrium is the most common intracardiac location of the tumor noted in 75% to 80% of patients, but it can also be found in the right atrium (10%-20%) or in the right or left ventricle (5%-10%).4 Although they are slow growing and typically not clinically significant until relatively large, myxomas can lead to an array of symptoms, largely depending on their location and severity.5,6First, they can obstruct flow from the right or left atrium to the ventricles, mimicking tricuspid or mitral stenosis. This can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath, syncope, and chest pain.7Second, they may grow large and be locally invasive, resulting in heart failure or arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation.6Third, they can embolize and travel to various organs of the body, either in part or whole.5,8Whereas left-sided myxomas embolize to the brain, kidneys, or other systemic vascular beds, right-sided myxomas are notorious for embolizing to the pulmonary arteries and lung.9These events can lead to dangerous complications, including stroke, kidney infarction, or pulmonary embolism. Performing a physical examination can be helpful when diagnosising atrial myxomas, with appreciation of an extra heart sound after S2 or a diastolic murmur. However, this strategy requires a thorough and detailed examination and is often overlooked.8 Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for detection of right atrial myxomas.3,6The peduncular appearance and nonhomogeneous characteristics with intermixed lucencies and calcifications are highly suggestive of the diagnosis.3This is in contrast to other intracardiac masses, such as lipomas or rhabdomyomas as well as thrombi, which are typically homogenous without peduncles. Cardiac computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and positron emission tomography have also been used to characterize myxomas but are more cumbersome to obtain and provide less functional information. Surgical resection of the tumor, its margins, and any embolic masses to the lung is the criterion standard of treatment for right atrial myxomas.4,7,8No specific pharmacologic therapies have been identified that target these tumors directly. Aspirin or anticoagulation therapies have not shown benefit for managing these tumors. The role of percutaneous catheter-directed thrombolytics has not been explored. However, recent studies have found an association between interleukin 6 or vascular endothelial growth factor and myxomas, holding promise for potential future targeted therapies.10 The patient was ultimately treated surgically with resection of the large primary right atrial myxoma. During the operative procedure, a second heterogeneous mass was also retrieved from the left pulmonary artery at the site of the computed tomography–visualized pulmonary embolism. On pathological examination, both masses were noted to be myxomatous, with myxoma cells and associated hemosiderin-laden macrophages and red blood cells (Figure 2). The patient felt notably improved after surgery, with resolution of his chest pain, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He was subsequently discharged from the hospital and, on follow-up with his outpatient cardiologist, remained symptom free with good exercise capacity.
